title: Lakes That Disappear
summary: Why lakes can shrink or vanish, from seasonal desert lakes and a lake that drains through a hole to the Aral Sea, and how a damaged lake can recover.
poll: People are the main reason that lakes disappear.

versions.title: Lakes That Go Away
versions.text:
A lake is a big pool of water. Land is all round it. Rain fills it up. So do streams. But a lake can lose some, too. The sun warms the lake. Bits of it go up in the air. We say it will evaporate.

What if more goes out than comes in? Then the lake will shrink. Some lakes dry up for good!

Some lakes come and go. In Saudi Arabia, there is not much rain. But a big storm can fill low land. A lake forms for a short time. Then the sun dries it up. White salt is left on the ground.

One lake in the USA has a hole in its floor. Each year, the lake drains out. Then it fills up once more.

We can make lakes shrink, too. The Aral Sea is a huge lake in Asia. Its rivers were used on farms. The farms grew cotton. Less water got to the lake. Most of it dried up. Ships were left on the sand!

Then a dam was built. Part of the lake grew back. Fish came back, too. We can help lakes. We can save water.

Then a dam was built. Part of the lake grew back. Fish came back, too. We can all help lakes by saving water.

versions.title: Lakes That Disappear
versions.text:
A lake is a large body of water with land all around it. Rain, melting snow, and rivers keep filling it up. At the same time, a lake is always losing water. The sun warms the surface, and some of the water rises into the air. We say the water will evaporate.

When more water leaves a lake than flows in, the lake begins to shrink. If this keeps happening, a lake can even disappear!

Some lakes come and go with the weather. Saudi Arabia gets very little rain. But after a heavy storm, water can fill low places in the desert. A shallow lake forms for a few weeks. Then the hot sun dries it up, and a crust of white salt is left on the ground.

In the United States, one lake has a hole in its floor. Every year, its water drains away into the ground. Later, rain and snow fill the lake again.

People can make lakes shrink, too. The Aral Sea in Asia was once one of the largest lakes in the world. About sixty years ago, farmers began to take water from its two rivers to grow cotton on their farms. Less and less water reached the lake, and most of it dried up. Fishing boats were left sitting on the sand! Strong winds blew salty dust from the dry ground, and people got sick.

Later, people built a dam to save the northern part of the lake. The water rose, and fish returned. Every person can help lakes by saving water.

versions.title: Lakes That Disappear
versions.text:
A lake is a large body of water surrounded by land. Rivers, rain, and melting snow add water to it. At the same time, a lake is always losing water. The sun heats the surface, and some of the water turns into a gas and rises into the air. This is called evaporation. Some water may also flow out through a river.

When more water leaves a lake than flows in, the lake begins to shrink. If this goes on for many years, a lake can disappear completely.

Some lakes appear and vanish naturally. These seasonal lakes are common in dry places. Saudi Arabia gets very little rain, but after a heavy storm, water can collect in low areas of the desert. A shallow lake may last for a few weeks. Then evaporation dries it up, and a crust of white salt is left on the ground.

In the state of Oregon, in the United States, a lake called Lost Lake has a hole in its floor. Every year, its water drains away underground. Later, rain and snow fill it again.

People can also cause lakes to shrink. The Aral Sea in Central Asia was once the fourth largest lake in the world. In the 1960s, farmers began taking water from its two rivers for irrigation. They used the water to grow cotton in the desert. Less and less water reached the lake, and most of it dried up. Fishing boats were left stranded on the sand. Strong winds picked up salty dust from the dry lakebed, and many people got sick.

In 2005, people finished a dam to save the northern part of the lake. The water rose, and fish began to return. The Aral Sea shows that lakes can recover when people use water wisely.

versions.title: Lakes That Disappear
versions.text:
A lake is a substantial body of water surrounded by land. Rivers, rainfall, and melting snow continually replenish it. Simultaneously, however, a lake is constantly losing water. Solar energy heats the surface, transforming some of the water into vapor that rises into the atmosphere, a process known as evaporation. Additional water may escape through an outflowing river.

Whenever more water leaves a lake than enters it, the lake begins to shrink. If this imbalance persists for many years, the lake can eventually disappear entirely.

Some lakes appear and vanish through entirely natural processes. Such seasonal lakes are common in arid regions. Saudi Arabia receives very little rainfall, but after a heavy storm, water can accumulate in low-lying areas of the desert, creating a shallow lake that may survive for several weeks. Eventually, evaporation removes the water, leaving a crust of white salt on the ground.

In the state of Oregon, in the United States, a lake called Lost Lake has an opening in its floor, which is connected to an underground tunnel formed long ago by volcanic activity. Every year, its water drains through this opening, and later, precipitation refills the basin.

Human decisions can also cause lakes to shrink, sometimes with serious consequences. The Aral Sea in Central Asia was once the fourth largest lake on Earth. Beginning in the 1960s, government planners decided to divert enormous quantities of water from its two major rivers for irrigation, so that farmers could cultivate cotton in the desert. Less and less water reached the lake, and most of it gradually evaporated. Fishing boats were left stranded on the sand. As the remaining water became increasingly salty, most of the native fish could no longer survive. Powerful winds carried salty, polluted dust from the exposed lakebed, contributing to serious health problems among local residents.

In 2005, engineers completed a dam to protect the northern portion of the lake. The water level rose, and fish gradually returned. Today, scientists also monitor vulnerable lakes using satellite photographs, which reveal how rapidly their shorelines are retreating. The Aral Sea demonstrates that damaged lakes can recover when communities adopt sustainable ways of managing water.

versions.title: Lakes That Disappear
versions.text:
A lake gains water from several sources, including rivers, rainfall, and melting snow, while simultaneously losing water through two main pathways: evaporation, in which sunlight heats the surface and slowly turns liquid water into vapor, and outflow through any rivers that drain away from the lake. When the combined losses from these pathways exceed the water the lake receives, the lake inevitably begins to shrink, and in extreme cases, it can vanish entirely.

Seasonal lakes are especially common across arid regions of the world. Saudi Arabia, for example, receives very little rainfall overall, yet occasional desert storms can still briefly fill low-lying areas with water, which subsequently evaporates and leaves behind a telltale white crust of salt across the dried lakebed. One striking example from elsewhere in the world is Lost Lake in Oregon, in the United States, whose floor contains an opening connected to an ancient volcanic underground tunnel. The lake drains away completely nearly every year through this opening, only to refill again each season as fresh precipitation arrives.

While seasonal disappearance driven by natural processes is one phenomenon, human activity can also cause far more serious and lasting consequences for a lake's survival. The Aral Sea, located in Central Asia, was once the fourth-largest lake on Earth, yet beginning in the 1960s, government planners made the fateful decision to divert water away from its two major feeder rivers in order to irrigate vast fields of cotton. The lake subsequently shrank at an alarming rate, stranding entire fishing boats on what had become dry sand, while the water that remained grew too salty to support the native fish population. Winds then carried salty, polluted dust from the newly exposed lakebed across the surrounding region, causing serious respiratory illness among nearby residents, a devastating consequence of the original irrigation decision.

There is, however, reason for cautious optimism. In 2005, the completion of a protective dam shielded the northern portion of the Aral Sea, allowing water levels there to rise once again and permitting fish populations to gradually return, clear evidence that even severely damaged lakes can partially recover when sustainable water management practices are properly implemented. Today, scientists closely monitor other vulnerable lakes around the world using satellite photographs. This allows them to detect early signs of a shrinking shoreline before the damage becomes irreversible, and hopefully to prevent other lakes from suffering the Aral Sea's grim fate. The broader lesson from the Aral Sea is that a consequence of diverting water for irrigation may not become visible for years, yet once a lake's balance between gains and losses tips too far toward evaporation and outflow, reversing the damage becomes extremely difficult and costly. For that reason, planners who irrigate farmland near any lake now weigh the long-term consequences far more carefully, treating sustainable water management as essential rather than optional.

versions.title: Lakes That Disappear
versions.text:
A lake gains water from several distinct sources, including feeder rivers, direct rainfall, and melting snow, while simultaneously losing water through two principal pathways: evaporation, a process in which sunlight heats the exposed surface and gradually converts liquid water into atmospheric vapor, and outflow through any rivers that continuously drain water away from the lake basin. Whenever the combined losses generated through these pathways exceed the total water the lake actually receives, the lake inevitably begins a gradual process of shrinkage, and in sufficiently extreme circumstances, it can ultimately vanish entirely from the landscape.

Seasonal lakes are especially prevalent across arid regions distributed throughout the world. Saudi Arabia, for example, receives extremely limited rainfall overall, yet occasional intense desert storms can nonetheless briefly fill low-lying depressions with water, which subsequently evaporates completely and leaves behind a telltale white crust of crystallized salt spread across the dried lakebed surface. A particularly striking illustrative example from elsewhere in the world is Lost Lake in Oregon, located within the United States, whose basin floor contains an opening connected directly to an ancient volcanic underground tunnel; the lake consequently drains away almost entirely nearly every single year through this geological opening, only to refill again reliably each subsequent season as fresh precipitation gradually arrives.

While seasonal disappearance driven purely by natural processes constitutes one distinct phenomenon, deliberate human activity can also produce far more serious and permanently lasting consequences for a lake's continued survival. The Aral Sea, located in Central Asia, was once recognized as the fourth-largest lake anywhere on Earth, yet beginning in the 1960s, government planners made the ultimately fateful decision to divert substantial water away from its two major feeder rivers specifically in order to irrigate vast agricultural fields devoted to cotton production. The lake subsequently shrank at an alarming and accelerating rate, stranding entire fishing boats upon what had rapidly become dry desert sand, while the comparatively small volume of water that remained grew far too saline to support the native fish population any longer. Prevailing winds then carried salty, chemically polluted dust from the newly exposed lakebed across the surrounding inhabited region, causing serious respiratory illness among nearby residents, a devastating and far-reaching consequence stemming directly from the original irrigation decision decades earlier.

There exists, however, legitimate reason for cautious optimism regarding such damaged ecosystems. In 2005, the completion of a protective engineered dam successfully shielded the northern portion of the Aral Sea, allowing local water levels there to rise meaningfully once again and permitting fish populations to gradually return to the recovering waters, clear and encouraging evidence that even severely damaged lakes can partially recover when genuinely sustainable water management practices are properly implemented and consistently maintained. Today, scientists worldwide closely monitor other similarly vulnerable lakes using detailed satellite photographs, allowing them to detect early warning signs of a shrinking shoreline well before the resulting damage becomes entirely irreversible, with the explicit hope of preventing other lakes elsewhere from ultimately suffering the Aral Sea's grim historical fate.

wrong.A: Fish were disappearing, not too many.
wrong.B: The dam helped the lake; it did not cause floods.
wrong.C: Cold mountain winds are not mentioned.

questions.stem: Why does a seasonal lake in Saudi Arabia leave a crust of salt behind?
options: People spread salt on the ground to keep it dry.
The salt stays when the water evaporates.
Sea waves carry salt into the desert.
The sun turns sand into salt.
questions.why: Evaporation removes only the water, so the salt that was mixed in the water stays on the ground.

wrong.A: The article does not say people spread salt.
wrong.C: These lakes form from rain, not sea waves.
wrong.D: The sun dries the water; it does not turn sand into salt.

questions.stem: Fish returned after the dam was built. What can you infer from this?
options: The fish needed more water to live there.
The fish preferred living in salty dust on the lakebed.
The dam was built to feed fish.
The fish came from Lost Lake.
questions.why: When the dam raised the water level, fish came back, so more water made the lake livable again.

wrong.B: Fish live in water, not dust.
wrong.C: The dam was built to protect the lake, not to feed fish.
wrong.D: Lost Lake is far away in the United States.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the article?
options: As the story of one family's trip to a lake
By listing lakes from largest to smallest
By explaining why lakes shrink, then giving natural and human examples
As a set of instructions for building a dam
questions.why: The article first explains how lakes gain and lose water, then describes seasonal lakes and Lost Lake, and then the Aral Sea.

wrong.B: The lakes are not listed by size.
wrong.D: The dam is mentioned, but the article gives no building steps.

MID.prompt: Explain two different reasons a lake can disappear. Use details from the article to support your answer.
checklist: I supported each reason with a detail from the article.
I used linking words such as because, also, and however.
MID.modelAnswer: One reason a lake can disappear is natural evaporation, because when the sun heats a seasonal lake faster than rain can refill it, the water dries up and only a crust of salt is left behind. Another reason is people taking too much water, because farmers diverted water for irrigation away from the rivers feeding the Aral Sea, and the lake shrank until boats were left stranded on dry sand. However, the article shows a lake can recover, since building a dam helped the northern Aral Sea's water level rise again and fish return.

keyWords.definition: the process by which a liquid turns into vapor
keyWords.example: In hot climates, evaporation from open reservoirs wastes a great deal of water.

keyWords.definition: the supply of water to land or crops through channels, pipes, or sprinklers
keyWords.example: Modern irrigation systems can deliver water directly to plant roots.

keyWords.definition: to change the direction or use of something
keyWords.example: Workers had to divert traffic while the bridge was repaired.

keyWords.definition: a result or effect of an action, often an important one
keyWords.example: One consequence of staying up late is feeling tired in class.

keyWords.definition: able to continue for a long time without harming the environment
keyWords.example: Planting trees is a sustainable way to protect soil from wind.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Lakes can vanish naturally or through human choices, yet some can recover.
Satellites are the best tool for studying deserts.
Cotton is the most important crop in Central Asia.
Seasonal lakes in Saudi Arabia are more valuable than the Aral Sea ever was.
questions.why: The article explains the water balance of lakes, gives natural and human examples of disappearing lakes, and ends with partial recovery.

wrong.B: Satellites are a supporting detail, and deserts are not the focus.
wrong.C: Cotton is part of the Aral Sea example, not the main idea.
wrong.D: The article does not rank the value of lakes.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is the opening in Lost Lake's floor connected to?
options: A river that carries its water all the way to the sea
A dam built by engineers
An underground tunnel formed by volcanic activity
A salt flat in the desert
questions.why: The article says the opening connects to an underground tunnel formed long ago by volcanic activity.

wrong.A: The water drains underground, not into a river.
wrong.B: The dam was built at the Aral Sea.
wrong.D: Salt crusts are described in Saudi Arabia, not at Lost Lake.

questions.stem: Why could most of the Aral Sea's native fish no longer survive?
options: The water became too cold.
Fishing boats caught every one of them before they could breed.
Satellites disturbed them.
The remaining water became too salty.
questions.why: The article says that as the remaining water became increasingly salty, most native fish could not survive.

wrong.A: Temperature is not given as the cause.
wrong.B: The boats were stranded on the sand.
wrong.C: Satellites only take photographs from space.

questions.stem: "Planners decided to divert enormous quantities of water." What does divert mean?
options: Purify
Redirect
Freeze
Measure
questions.why: The water was sent away from the lake to cotton fields, so divert means to change its direction or use.

wrong.D: Measuring water would not make the lake shrink.

questions.stem: What was a direct result of diverting the rivers that fed the Aral Sea?
options: The lake grew larger.
Less water reached the lake, so it shrank.
Cotton farming in the region stopped completely within a year.
The northern dam was destroyed.
questions.why: Because water was taken for irrigation, less reached the lake and most of it evaporated.

wrong.C: The water was diverted to grow cotton.
wrong.D: The dam was built later to help the lake.

questions.stem: Why would scientists use satellite photographs to monitor lakes?
options: To decide where to grow cotton
To find the hidden opening in the floor of Lost Lake
To count fish in the water
To notice early when a lake is shrinking
questions.why: The photographs reveal how quickly shorelines are retreating, so people can see problems early and respond.

wrong.A: The article links satellites to protecting lakes, not to farming.
wrong.B: The opening is underground, so photos from space would not reveal it.
wrong.C: Satellite photos show shorelines, not individual fish.

questions.stem: Based on the article, which situation would most likely make a lake grow?
options: Years of heavy rain while less river water is taken for farms
A long, hot period with no rain
New irrigation canals from its rivers
A new opening in its floor
questions.why: A lake grows when more water enters than leaves, and both more rain and less irrigation would add water.

wrong.B: Heat and no rain increase evaporation and reduce supply.
wrong.C: Irrigation canals take water away, as at the Aral Sea.
wrong.D: An opening lets water drain away, as at Lost Lake.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with the dam completed in 2005?
options: To argue that every lake needs a dam
To describe how cotton is harvested
To show that damage to a lake can be partly reversed
To explain how seasonal lakes form
questions.why: After the dam, the water rose and fish returned, showing that sustainable choices can help a damaged lake recover.

wrong.A: The author does not claim all lakes need dams.

HIGH.prompt: Farmers need water, and lakes need water too. How should a community decide how to share its water? Support your opinion with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my opinion.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I believe a community should share its water sustainably, balancing farmers' need for irrigation with the lake's own need for water to survive. The Aral Sea shows the consequence of ignoring this balance: when farmers diverted its rivers for cotton irrigation in the 1960s, the lake shrank so much that fishing boats were stranded on dry sand and people got sick from salty dust blown off the dry lakebed. On the other hand, the article shows that building a dam in 2005 let water and fish return to part of the lake, proving that careful, planned water use can let both farms and lakes survive together.
